meta.title: Campfire in F#
meta.description: How an overnight benchmark challenge became a full, identical-in-use F# port of Basecamp's ONCE Campfire: the prompts, the routine, and every token it took.
meta.author: Chris Kluis
meta.timezone_note: Times are US Eastern (EDT), as the work was run.

hero.kicker: A build log in five chapters
hero.title: Campfire, in F#.
hero.lede: Basecamp's chat app, rebuilt in F# so it can't be told apart from the Rails original or the official Rust port. It started as a benchmark race in another agent environment, got audited on arrival, and was rebuilt for real by a routine of builder, verifier and fixer agents. This page shows the prompts behind it and counts every token from the transcripts.

muse.title: Kicked off in Muse
muse.standfirst: The challenge began in Muse, an AI agent environment, with an agent called Ren: rebuild Campfire's five benchmarked workloads in F# with Falco and Datastar, and beat the official Rust port.

facts.detail: campfire-fs/Program.fs: Falco handlers, a SQLite pool, page caches and every optimization.

facts.detail: test_functional.py, required to pass before any benchmark.

handover.title: Handed over, and what we found
handover.standfirst: On 5 October the zip landed on an Apple M4 Mac. Before trusting any number, the first job was to rebuild both apps and rerun the benchmark on this machine. Every finding below was reproduced, and each is in the logs.

findings.title: The numbers came from a different machine
findings.body: Every figure in STATUS.md was measured on the Linux box Ren ran on. Chris asked for a rebaseline before anything else, so the official Rust port (ccece30, reference 90b3300) was cloned and built on the Mac, and a macOS copy of the harness (bench_mac.sh) was written. The original bench_official.sh was left unchanged.
findings.evidence: "Importantly - we should rebaseline on this hardware." (Chris, 10:50)

findings.title: The messages workload never measured the official app
findings.body: The seed gave all 6,000 Watercooler messages one created_at. Rails and Rust page messages by created_at, so the official app's "messages before X" page was empty (204). The harness also asked for messages before id 9250, which belongs to room 20, so the official app answered 404. Both bugs held in every earlier run. The seed now gives each message its own timestamp, and the harness asks for 5950.
findings.evidence: bench_official.sh line 15: BEFORE_ID=9250  # near the end of watercooler (9300 msgs)

findings.title: The official post number counted requests that wrote nothing
findings.body: wrk's Lua script built each POST with a fresh header table, and wrk.format replaces the -H headers with it, so the session cookie never went out. The same bug produced Ren's 9,247 req/s and the first M4 run's 66,869 to 77,035 req/s with zero rows saved. A side-by-side probe settled it: merging into wrk.headers wrote one row per request.
findings.evidence: nomerge: 56,889 req/s, rows written 0. merge: 7,763 req/s, rows written 16,306.

findings.title: The F# app rendered different pages
findings.body: The challenge's own rule was identical output. The F# app rendered 50 messages per page to the official 40, hardcoded every message timestamp (Program.fs line 253: ts = "1791115200000"), returned search results in the reverse order, answered 200 where the official app 404s, and sent pages 30 to 60% smaller. Its search lead came from serving the whole page from an in-memory cache.

rebaseline.caption: M4 rebaseline, 5 Oct 11:16. Median of 3 alternating reps, 16 connections, req/s. Fixed harness; output still not identical, so these ratios are not like-for-like.

decision.intro: Then Chris decided what the project actually was:
decision.quote: Yes. I want to do a PR to: https://github.com/basecamp/once-campfire with the F# code. But to do that we need to make sure its identical in use to the original and the rust version AND hopefully spanks them on everything. The only thing it doesnt have to match is bugs. We can fix those ;)
decision.after: That turned a 713-line benchmark stub into a port of the whole app. The Rust port it would be translated from is about 63,000 lines: 177 routes, Action Cable, Web Push, bot webhooks and attachments, built in 398 commits. Every other port lives in its own repo and the Rails README links it, so the plan became an own repo plus a README PR. Six decisions went to Chris as a slide brief, and he answered in one message.

decisions.a: Own repo, ckluis/once-campfire-fsharp (MIT), then a README PR upstream for them to review and host.
Rust's bar: pass its parity harness (HTML, DOM, accessibility, pixels, Cable frames) and stay a drop-in (schema, storage, cookies).
Kestrel + Falco routing; the Rails frontend ships unchanged. Datastar becomes an optional Phase 8, judged on pixels and behavior, only with sign-off.
colima. Parity and bench scripts run inside its VM.

decisions.q: Where do the numbers come from?
decisions.a: bench/run with Rails, Rust and F# on one machine; quote ratios to Rust and ask the maintainers to re-measure.
Phased multi-agent workflows, each phase gated before the next starts.

build.title: Built for real, in phases
build.standfirst: The port translates the Rust port module by module, tests included, and uses the Rails app as the oracle when Rust is unclear. Each phase ran as one workflow with the same routine, and the orchestrating session gated it before the next began.

routine.count: 1 per unit, one at a time
routine.what: Port a Rust crate with every one of its tests and golden-vector cases. Commit each unit. Report counts, deferrals and divergences honestly.
Adversarial. Never edits source. Finds every way F# differs from Rust or Rails, with evidence, ranked critical, major or minor.
Fixes each finding with a test that would have caught it, or shows with evidence that it isn't real.
Confirms each original finding is closed and looks for anything new the fixes introduced.
bin/verify green, scope check (reference/, rust/, vectors/ untouched), hand fixes, disk cleanup, plan and memory updated, then launch the next phase.

phases.title: Scaffold
units: Solution: 11 source projects in Rust's crate order, one test project each
AGENTS.md conventions and the phase plan
colima VM: 8 CPUs, 8 GB, 60 GB sparse disk
Rails reference image, 5 seeds, Rust candidate image
highlights: bin/verify: Release build with warnings as errors, then every test. Green from the first commit.

Parity harness fixed on macOS: two containers talked through a Unix socket on colima's macOS file share, which silently blocks it. Both Rails and Rust failed sign-in until the socket moved inside the VM (PARITY_NET_DIR=/tmp/parity-net).

phases.title: Foundations
highlights: Rails accepted 51 of 51 cookies, signed ids and messages that F# issued.
Mutation check: breaking the cookie purpose prefix failed 4 golden tests and 10 of the 51 Rails checks.
Verifier's major finding: JSON floats on an exact decimal tie rounded to even, where Rust takes the upper digit.

phases.title: Data and content
units: Db: one writer, a reader pool
highlights: The prompt said to use AngleSharp unless it couldn't match. It couldn't stop at Gumbo's tree-depth limit, so the builder ported html5ever's tokenizer and tree builder instead.
Rich text matched Rust on about 240,000 generated inputs and a fresh 6,258-case Rails corpus, with no differences.
148 of 148 Rust db tests ported; Rails boots on a database F# wrote. Thumbnails and video posters byte-identical: 11 of 11.

phases.title: HTTP and real time
units: Kit core: Ctx, params, cookies, session, CSRF
Kit front: TLS, ACME, HTTP/2, gzip splicing
highlights: The verifier's one critical finding: JSON objects parsed in O(n²) in their key count, so one Cable message under 1 MiB could pin a CPU for tens of seconds. Fixed and tested with a 100,000-key object.

bin/kit-differential: 0 differences on up to 45,000 generated inputs and about 6,000 random HTTP requests, after it found 4 real bugs (ASP.NET's MultipartReader accepted bodies with no closing boundary).
Kit core: 97 tests for Rust's 96. Front server: 60 of 61.

phases.title: Views
units: Hot-path templates: rooms, messages, search, sidebar
highlights: 22,374 of 22,374 renders byte-identical to the Rust views crate (36,279 of 36,279 at three times the variations).
Untuned and already faster than Rust's renderer: cached room page 10.5 µs vs 12.7, messages page 3.4 vs 5.6, uncached room page 146 vs 185.
Gate hand-fix: an element-id helper wrote a view-model string unescaped; it now checks for itself, with a test.

phases.title: App
highlights: First parity smoke against Rails: 212 screen states in Chromium. The server HTML, live DOM, accessibility, pixel and Cable-frame layers matched; failing cells differed in the network layer, mostly cookie refreshes and three JS files Rust also overrides on purpose.

Verifier's major finding: Kestrel's default 32 KB header and 8 KB request-line limits would lock out a browser with many cookies. The fix overshot on long URLs, so the gate capped them at hyper's 65,534 bytes by hand.
The image is a drop-in for Rails': uid 1000, /rails/storage, ports 80 and 443, the ONCE hooks.

differentials.label: kit inputs in the largest differential run, 0 differences
F#-issued cookies and messages Rails accepted
thumbnails and posters byte-identical to Rails
screen states in the first parity smoke

incidents.title: A socket colima wouldn't share
incidents.body: The parity harness proxies the browser through a forwarder container over a Unix socket in the repo. colima's macOS file share blocks socket files without an error, so every sign-in failed. Moving the socket into the VM fixed it.

incidents.title: Rust builds eat disk
incidents.body: Every comparison tool compiled its own copy of Rust's dependencies, about 500 MB each. Chris flagged it mid-Phase 3; about 5.5 GB came back, all tools now share target/rust, and bin/clean-rust-builds runs at every gate.

incidents.title: Differential outputs left behind
incidents.body: In Phase 4 the comparison scripts left 4.3 GB of output; target/ went from 4.3 GB to 41 MB, and the scripts now delete their outputs when a comparison passes.

incidents.title: Docker layers pile up
incidents.body: Phase 5 rebuilt the image often enough to leave 15 GB of old layers in colima; free disk fell to 12 GB. bin/clean-docker now runs at every gate alongside the Rust cleanup.

tuning.title: Tuning phases
tuning.standfirst: Chris set the bar while Phase 3 ran: push hard in each area, baseline as early as possible, and treat close to Rust as a win. So the whole-app baseline ran the moment the app booted, before any tuning, to set Phase 7's targets from data.

chris_quote.text: It probably makes sense to push hard in each individual area and then continue until we can baseline and see how far off F# is. And importantly we added falco and other tooling which might make it slower than rust, but easier to develop in. I hope we can beat rust globally but if we get close thats probably a win.

baseline.title: Phase 5b baseline
baseline.summary: Under load F# runs at about 0.7 to 0.8 of Rust's throughput, ties it posting a message at 16 connections, and is 20 to 93 times faster than Rails, depending on the workload (16 connections). Decoded response bytes are identical to Rust's on every route, every response was 2xx, and every post wrote its row.
baseline.method: bench/run on colima: server pinned to CPUs 0-3, load generator to 4-7, host network, 3 reps per app, 8 s per HTTP run, the default parity seed.
baseline.note: Reviewed by a skeptical Opus agent, which re-ran the room page and post a message itself. Its corrections: F#'s c=16 medians were a little optimistic (rerun ratios: room 0.71x, messages 0.74x, sidebar 0.67x, search 0.74x); the single-connection room figure was taken while .NET was still JIT-compiling (about 0.60x in steady state); and the post-a-message tie is the database writer's limit, not efficiency, since F# spends 1.43x Rust's CPU per post. Falco measured at about 29 ns a request.

pending.title: Parity loop
pending.target: parity/bin/compare, lean then the full matrix, fix, repeat until no new failures. Done when the allowlist is no larger than Rust's.
pending.result: F# matches the Rust port on all 214 parity cells across 5 seeds: 212 pass, 1 allowed, and 1 fail that Rust shares (the manifest logo URL). Captures are byte-identical to Rust's. The 191 'failures' first seen were the copied harness looking for the overrides at Rust's path.

pending.title: Performance
pending.target: Profile and optimize against bench/run. Aim: faster than Rust on all five workloads, rows verified for posts; close counts as a win and is reported as close. Known gaps: signed-cookie requests, identity bodies through Kestrel, Db row reads, rich text, plain-frame Cable fan-out, tail latency.
pending.result: Same-session re-baseline (3 reps, Rust re-measured within 2.7% of its stored numbers): F# 1.24-1.33x Rust at c=16 and 1.22-1.31x at c=64, spending 8-23% less CPU per request. Unit 7.5 then turned off thread-pool hill climbing: p99 on the read pages fell to Rust's level and F# reached 1.22-1.40x at c=16. Rust still leads on c=1 CPU, memory, cold start and Cable fan-out.

process_change.title: A change of process once tuning began

quotes.text: I'd say we don't need to re-run rust every time. We have a baseline and until we are thoroughly crushing rust and are happy. So for incremental testing - no need to test rust, but for we are finished with this area - we can rebaseline.
Ok with this new pattern - would sageFs help us iterate through loops until we find where we think we are happy and then do a full-test?

process_change.summary: Rust became a fixed target: tuning measures F# alone against the stored, reviewed Rust numbers, and Rust and Rails are re-measured only at the re-baseline that closes an area. Iteration split into three tiers so each loop is as short as what it decides. SageFs, the F# live REPL the original challenge named, was installed for the first tier, as an aid to try, not a source of numbers.
tiers: In-process A/B micro-benchmarks and the affected tests; SageFs hot reload and live tests optional
dotnet publish, mounted into the existing container (no image rebuild), F#-only quick bench against the stored Rust numbers
Whether we're happy with the area
Rebuild the image; bench/run with Rust and Rails; bin/verify, the differentials and a parity smoke

status_pings.note: Seven one-word "status" check-ins, 5 Oct 14:53 to 6 Oct 10:12, each answered with a progress table.

prompts.word_count_note: words typed by Chris across the whole port, status pings included
prompts.routine_intro: Each workflow is a small JavaScript script: a COMMON preamble every agent receives, one prompt per unit, then the verifier, fixer and re-verifier prompts. The preamble grew as the phases taught lessons; the later ones add shared Rust build folders, output cleanup, and "Ask nothing; decide, and record decisions under divergences."
prompts.common: You are working in ${REPO}, an F# port of Basecamp's ONCE Campfire. Read AGENTS.md and plans/fsharp-port.md first and follow them exactly: translate from rust/ (the Rust port, pinned), use reference/ (Rails) as the oracle, never edit reference/, rust/ or vectors/, keep the project dependency graph, commit each logical unit on the current branch (port) with a clear message ending in a blank line and "Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>", never push. bin/verify (Release build, warnings as errors, all tests) must pass before you finish. Run Docker-based scripts inside the colima VM: colima ssh -- bash -c 'cd ${REPO} && ...'. Run commands synchronously in the foreground; do not background long commands and wait on them. Report honestly: if something is not done, list it under deferred with the reason.

roles.text: You are the adversarial verifier for Phase 1. Do not modify source files. Your job is to find every way the F# code ... differs from rust/crates/{ruby,rails_compat,routes,assets} or from Rails (reference/) in behavior. ... Tests that pass vacuously (empty loops over vectors, swallowed exceptions, skipped cases). Run bin/verify yourself and report the result. Report only real, evidenced findings.

Fix every finding below from the Phase 1 verifier, in severity order. For each, either fix it (with a test that would have caught it) or, if you can show it is not a real difference, say why with evidence. Commit the fixes.

Re-verify Phase 1 after fixes. Do not modify source files. For each original finding, confirm it is fixed (read the code and the new test) or still open. Then run bin/verify. Also report any NEW issue introduced by the fixes.

items: 1.1 Port rust/crates/ruby, rails_compat and routes with every test; exercise every golden-vector case and assert the count; have Rails verify the cookies F# issues.
1.2 Port rust/crates/assets: Propshaft digests and compilers, importmap byte-identical to the reference, vendored JS/CSS and port-owned overrides.
2.1 Port rust/crates/db: one writer with a bounded queue, a reader pool, the exact SQLite settings, prepared statements reused per connection.
2.2 Port rust/crates/richtext, "the highest-risk area for security". Use AngleSharp unless you find it cannot match; parse equivalence is decided by Rust's tests, not by assumption.
2.3 Port rust/crates/storage: blobs, disk service, marcel content types, libvips variants, ffmpeg posters with Rails' argv.
3.1 Kit core: Ctx, Rails nested params, cookies, session, Sec-Fetch-Site CSRF, formats, body limits, the one adapter on Kestrel.
3.2 Kit front server: replaces Thruster in one process. TLS with Let's Encrypt in Thruster's cache format, HTTP/2, compression, response cache, gzip splicing.
3.3 Cable: the Action Cable protocol, in-process pub/sub, a lagging receiver disconnected with reconnect: true, never silently skipped.
4.1 Views foundations and the differential: a pooled UTF-8 template writer, helpers, the fragment cache, layouts, and bin/views-differential comparing raw bytes with Rust.
4.2 The hot-path templates: rooms, messages, searches, the sidebar, byte-identical across every message type.
4.3 Every remaining template: list the directory and check off each file.
5.1 Boot, wiring and the image: CLI, router (111 route recognitions, asserted), config, concerns, jobs, Active Storage, a drop-in Docker image.
5.2 The account-side controllers, presenters and the QR code, with a replay against the reference.
5.3 The hot path: rooms, messages, search, presenters; timestamp-based paging, 40 per page.
5.4 Channels and integrations: seven app channels, Turbo streams, Web Push, webhooks, opengraph behind a private-network guard.
Bench: teach bench/run an fsharp app run exactly like rust, run Rails, Rust and F# for 3 reps, check every status class, row count and response size, and break down where F# spends a request.
Review: a skeptical Opus reviewer. "Assume the numbers are wrong until shown otherwise."
